sermon:
## Chosen Before the Foundation: Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ (Ephesians 1:1-14)
*Why the Christian's account was settled before the Christian existed*

**Text:** Ephesians 1:1-14 · **Supporting:** John 15:16 · Romans 8:29-30 · 2 Timothy 1:9 · Titus 3:5 · 1 Peter 1:3-5 · Revelation 13:8

You cannot earn a gift that was given before you were born. That is the offense of this passage, and if you have spent any time inside a post-Christian culture, it is an offense you have been trained to resist. We are raised now to believe the self is a project. You build it, you optimize it, you curate it, you earn every good thing it possesses. The whole architecture of the modern person assumes that what you are is what you achieved. Grace does not fit that world. Grace hands you an inheritance while you are still dead, still ungrateful, still organizing your whole life around an absence you could not name. Paul opens his letter to a small church in a port city on the Aegean coast and does something no self-help culture will ever do. He tells them the story is already finished, and they were not the ones who finished it.

### I. The Father Chose, Before You Drew a Breath (Ephesians 1:3-6)
Paul writes what is, in the Greek, a single unbroken sentence from verse 3 through verse 14, one long doxology that refuses to pause, as if the man could not find a place to breathe. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ" (Ephesians 1:3). Every blessing. Already given. Past tense. The verb *eulogēsas* is aorist, a finished act, not an ongoing negotiation. Whatever the believer will ever need has already been deposited, and the deposit is in Christ, never in the self. Read the phrase "in Christ" through this passage and you will find it eleven times in twelve verses. Everything Paul is about to celebrate is located in one place, and that place is not you.

Then Paul locates the source. "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love" (Ephesians 1:4). Before the foundation of the world. Before Eden, before the fall, before you had a name or a wound or a résumé. The word is *exelexato*, he selected, he picked out for himself, middle voice, God choosing for God's own sake. Jesus told the disciples the same thing in the upper room: "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you" (John 15:16). Paul is not inventing a doctrine. He is repeating his Lord. And the aim of the choosing is not merely rescue but holiness, "that we should be holy and without blame." Election is not a warrant to coast. It is a call to become what you were chosen to be.

- **A. Election is not cold; it is love running upstream.** Verse 5 says God predestined us "unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will." *Huiothesia*, adoption, the legal act of a Roman father taking a child who was not his by blood and giving him the full name and the full inheritance. This is not the language of a factory sorting parts. It is the language of a father crossing a room to claim a child. This is the answer to the father-hunger that sits under so many broken lives, not that you found a father, not that you performed your way into a family, but that a Father chose you first, before you could do anything to deserve it or anything to ruin it.
- **B. The purpose is his glory, not your comfort.** Three times Paul lands the same refrain like a bell: "to the praise of the glory of his grace" (v. 6), "that we should be to the praise of his glory" (v. 12), "unto the praise of his glory" (v. 14). We want a gospel arranged around us, our healing, our best life, our felt needs. This one is arranged around him. And strangely, that is the only version that can hold your weight. A gospel centered on you collapses the moment you do. A gospel centered on his glory stands when you cannot.

### II. The Son Redeemed, and the Spirit Sealed (Ephesians 1:7-14)
Election would be a terror if it stopped at the Father's hidden will. It does not stop there. It comes out of eternity and lands in history, at a specific cross. "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace" (Ephesians 1:7). *Apolutrōsis*, the price paid to free a slave from the auction block, the ransom that buys a captive out of bondage. The choosing was eternal, but it was not cheap. It ran through blood. Peter names the same ledger: "ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Peter 1:18-19). And John, given a vision of the end, looks back to the beginning and sees a Lamb "slain from the foundation of the world" (Revelation 13:8). The cross was not the divine backup plan after Eden went wrong. It was the plan, older than the dirt.

Then the third movement, and the whole Trinity has now acted. "In whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession" (Ephesians 1:13-14). Two ancient images stack here. A *sphragis* was the wax seal pressed on a document or a shipment to mark ownership and guarantee it would arrive intact. The Spirit is God's seal on you, his mark of ownership, his guarantee of delivery. And the Spirit is the *arrabōn*, the down payment, the first installment of a purchase that legally obligates the buyer to complete the rest. In modern Greek the same word came to mean an engagement ring. The Spirit in you is God's pledge that he will finish what he started. Paul told Timothy the whole thing was settled the same way: God "hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began" (2 Timothy 1:9).

- **A. Three persons, one saving act.** The Father chooses, the Son redeems, the Spirit seals. Not three gods with three agendas, one God, one purpose, one people, secured at every link in the chain Paul lays out in Romans: "whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate... whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified" (Romans 8:29-30). Every verb past tense. Nothing hanging, nothing conditional, no link where your effort could snap the chain.
- **B. The seal is what lets you rest.** Titus 3:5 says he saved us "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy." If the Spirit sealed you, no failure of yours breaks the seal, because you did not press it and you cannot lift it. Peter says the same inheritance is "reserved in heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God" (1 Peter 1:4-5). Kept. Not keeping yourself. Kept.

### III. Living Well When You Own Nothing You Earned
Here is the confession. I have preached this passage and then walked out of the room and lived like a man auditioning for a job I already have. I have treated the Christian life like a performance review, tallying my own devotion, wondering if I had done enough that week to keep God warm toward me, as though the God who chose me before the foundation of the world could be talked out of it by a bad Tuesday. And I have watched congregants do the same, good people, exhausted people, adding chariots to a covenant that was already secure, trusting their own consistency the way Israel trusted Egypt. We believe the doctrine on Sunday and deny it with our anxiety by Thursday.

The church has fought this exact fight before, and it nearly lost. By the early 1500s the whole machinery of Western Christianity ran on the assumption that grace was a substance you accumulated and could run short of, a treasury you drew from, paid into, and worried over. A monk named Martin Luther, terrified of a God he could not appease no matter how he fasted or confessed, read Paul and discovered that the righteousness of God was not a wage he had to earn but a gift he could only receive. On October 31, 1517, he nailed ninety-five theses to a door in Wittenberg. What people remember as a protest against corruption was, at its root, a recovery of this sentence in Ephesians, that the blessing is already given, in full, in Christ, before you moved a muscle.

And the reason it is already given is the man in verse 7. The choosing in eternity had to become blood in time. God did not simply decide to love you at a safe distance and leave you there. He entered the room where you were dying and paid what you could not pay. The election that feels so cold and abstract on the page has a body and a cross. If you want to know whether God chose you in love or merely in decree, look at Golgotha, where the choosing bled.

- **A. Stop auditing what God has sealed.** If you are still trying to earn the standing you already hold, you are, with your anxiety, quietly calling God a liar. Rest is not laziness here. Rest is faith taking God at his word about the seal.
- **B. Live for the praise of his glory, not the maintenance of your worth.** A person still trying to establish his value will use every relationship as a mirror and every good deed as a payment. A person who is already secure, chosen, redeemed, sealed, is finally free to love without keeping score. This is why the doctrine of election, which strikes so many as cold and forbidding, is in fact the warmest thing in the letter. It means your standing before God does not rise and fall with your performance, because it never rested on your performance to begin with. The exhausted believer, forever auditioning, is not too spiritual. He has simply not yet believed verse 4.

Nothing was left for you to earn.

## The Prayer for Open Eyes: Knowing the Power That Raised Christ (Ephesians 1:15-23)
*Paul asks not for more, but for sight to see what the church already owns*

**Text:** Ephesians 1:15-23 · **Supporting:** Colossians 2:9-10 · Romans 8:11 · 2 Kings 6:17 · John 17:3 · Philippians 3:10 · Colossians 1:18

Paul has just spent one long, breathless sentence telling this church they possess every spiritual blessing there is. So what does he pray for next? Nothing. He asks for no new blessing at all. He asks that they be able to see the ones they already have. That is a strange prayer in a culture built on acquisition, where the assumption is always that the thing you lack is the thing you need, and the answer to any ache is more, more experience, more possessions, more self-knowledge, more. Paul assumes the opposite. He assumes the Ephesians are like a man who inherited a fortune and lives like a pauper because he never opened the letter. The problem is not poverty. The problem is blindness. And blindness is the one poverty you cannot fix by getting more, you can pile riches on a blind man and he will still stumble in the dark, because his lack was never in his hands but in his eyes.

### I. Paul Prays for Sight, Not Supply (Ephesians 1:15-18)
"Wherefore I also, after I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints, cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers" (Ephesians 1:15-16). He starts with thanksgiving, because he has already told them what they have. Then comes the request itself: "that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: the eyes of your understanding being enlightened" (Ephesians 1:17-18).

The phrase in verse 18 is arresting once you see the Greek behind the translation. The eyes of your *kardia*, the heart. The ancients did not locate thinking in the head alone; the heart was the seat of the whole inner person, the mind and will and affections together. Paul is praying for the illumination of the deepest self, because the knowledge he wants for them is not data. It is *epignōsis*, knowledge that grips and changes, the intimate, personal knowing Jesus meant when he prayed, "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" (John 17:3). Not know about. Know. You can know about a person from a file. You know a person from a shared life. Paul is asking for the second kind, aimed at God himself.

- **A. The great need is not information but revelation.** You can hold a true doctrine in your head and be stone dead to it in your heart. Paul is not asking that the Ephesians learn something new; he is asking that God open their eyes over truths they can already recite. The most dangerous condition in the church is not ignorance. It is the familiarity that has stopped seeing, the Christian who can define grace precisely and has not been undone by it in years. Sound theology can become a museum you walk through without ever being moved. This is why Paul, of all people, prays for revelation over a church he has already taught. He knew that teaching alone does not open eyes; only God opens eyes, and so the man who had more to say about the gospel than almost anyone who ever lived spent his time on his knees asking God to make his own students see what he had told them.
- **B. There is a servant in the Old Testament who saw this happen.** The prophet Elisha and his servant woke one morning to find the city of Dothan ringed by the Syrian army, horses, chariots, a host sent to capture the prophet. The servant panicked and cried out. Elisha prayed a strange prayer over him: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha" (2 Kings 6:17). Nothing about the situation changed. Not one Syrian soldier left. The only thing that changed was the servant's sight, and everything changed. The armies of heaven had been there the whole time. That is exactly the prayer Paul is praying over a church that already has more than it can see.

### II. Three Things to See, Hope, Inheritance, Power (Ephesians 1:18-23)
Paul names the three specific things he wants their opened eyes to take in. "That ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe" (Ephesians 1:18-19). Hope, inheritance, power, the future secured, the wealth owned, the strength available.

The third one is where the sentence detonates. Paul refuses to leave "power" as a vague spiritual mood, so he measures it against a fixed and staggering benchmark: "according to the working of his mighty power, which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 1:19-20). Read the units of measurement. He stacks four different Greek words for power in these verses, *dunamis*, *energeia*, *kratos*, *ischus*, as though one word could not carry the load and he had to pile them up. And then he anchors the whole immeasurable quantity to a single event. The power at work in you is resurrection power, the same force that reached into a sealed tomb, dragged a corpse out of death, and seated it over the entire universe. Paul says the same elsewhere without flinching: "the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwelleth in you" (Romans 8:11). This is why he could ache, near the end of his life, "that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings" (Philippians 3:10). He already had the power. He wanted to know it.

- **A. The inheritance runs both directions.** Notice the odd phrase most readers skim past, "the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints." Read it slowly. It is not only your inheritance in God. It is God's inheritance in you. The church is not only the heir; the church is the treasure God counts as his own portion. You are not merely a beneficiary named in the will. You are a line item in it, something God considers glorious to possess. A person raised without being wanted spends a lifetime trying to become wanted. Paul says God already counts you as his glory.
- **B. Christ is seated over everything, and he is your head.** Paul finishes the sentence at the throne: God "hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all" (Ephesians 1:22-23). Colossians says it as plainly as it can be said, "in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power" (Colossians 2:9-10), for "he is the head of the body, the church" (Colossians 1:18). The one seated above every authority in the universe is joined to you as a head is joined to a body. His victory is not a rumor arriving from a distant throne. It runs down the spine into the members.

### III. Living Well When You Already Own What You Cannot See
I have prayed for the wrong things for most of my ministry. I have prayed the way a post-Christian consumer prays without knowing it, send me more, fix this circumstance, supply that lack, change these people, adjust these conditions and then I will be well. I have rarely prayed Paul's prayer, which asks for nothing new and everything I have already been given and simply cannot see. That is a confession, not a technique. The modern church does not mostly suffer from a shortage of blessing. It suffers from a shortage of sight, and a person standing in the middle of chariots of fire can still die of despair if his eyes stay shut.

There is a moment in the fourth century worth naming precisely. A brilliant, restless African named Augustine spent years convinced the answer to his hunger was somewhere he had not yet looked, more philosophy, more experience, more pleasure, more acquisition, always somewhere out ahead of him. In the summer of 386, in a garden in Milan, he heard a child's voice through a wall chanting "take up and read," opened the Scriptures to Romans, and was undone. Later, in his *Confessions* written around 397, he addressed God with a line that could serve as a footnote to this whole passage: "You were within me, and I was in the external world and sought you there." He had been searching outside for what was already inside the letter, already sealed in his own chest. That is the human condition, and it is the Ephesian condition, and it is ours.

And the sight Paul prays for is not finally about seeing our blessings. It is about seeing him, the risen, enthroned, present Christ who is the content of every blessing named. The prayer bends, as all true prayer does, away from the gift and toward the Giver.

- **A. Ask God to open your eyes before you ask him to change your circumstances.** The circumstances you are begging him to remove may be your chariots of fire, and you simply cannot see them yet. Sometimes the answer to the prayer is not a new situation but a new set of eyes on the old one.
- **B. Measure your power by the empty tomb, not by your feelings.** The same force that raised Christ from the dead is the force at work in you who believe. Your sense of weakness on a given morning does not repeal the resurrection. Feelings are weather. The tomb is fact. The Christian who lives defeated is not, usually, a Christian without power. He is a Christian who has never had his eyes opened to the power he was given, staring at his own inadequacy while the chariots of fire burn unseen on the hill. The prayer for such a person is not for more. It is for sight, and it is a prayer God delights to answer.

You already have what you cannot see.

## Dead, Then Alive: Grace From First Breath to Last (Ephesians 2:1-10)
*Why the resurrection you need most is the one you cannot perform*

**Text:** Ephesians 2:1-10 · **Supporting:** Colossians 2:13 · Romans 5:8 · John 5:24 · Titus 3:5 · Romans 9:16 · 1 Corinthians 15:10

There is a word in a culture obsessed with self-improvement that no self-improvement culture can survive. The word is *dead*. Not sick. Not struggling. Not underperforming. Not a work in progress. Dead. You cannot coach a corpse. You cannot motivate it, incentivize it, put it on a plan, or send it to a better program. A corpse has no potential to draw out because a corpse has nothing left. And Paul opens the second chapter of Ephesians by telling a room full of religious people that this, precisely this, is what they were. Everything the post-Christian world teaches you to believe about yourself, that you are basically good, that you already hold the raw material of your own rescue, that with the right tools and enough will you can build the life you want, dies on the first word of this passage. And it dies not with a sneer but with a mercy, because a lie about your condition, however flattering, can only ever lead you to the wrong cure.

### I. The Diagnosis: Dead, Walking, Doomed (Ephesians 2:1-3)
"And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1). *Nekros*, a corpse, the same word used for a body in a grave. Paul does not say we were leaning the wrong direction or running low. He says we were dead, and then he lays out the anatomy of the death. "Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:2). Three tyrants held us at once: the world's downstream current pulling us along, the devil's active governance over the disobedient, and, verse 3, the flesh's own appetite. "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others."

Read that last phrase slowly. *By nature the children of wrath.* Not by accident. Not by a handful of bad choices we could have reversed with better information. By nature, it was what we were, not merely what we did. The problem was not on the surface, where a program could reach it; it was in the root. Paul says the same to the Colossians: "And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). Dead, then quickened. The order matters, because the dead do not contribute to their own resurrection.

- **A. The flattering diagnosis cannot save you.** Every therapy that begins by telling you that you are already whole, already enough, already holding the answer within, is prescribing for the wrong disease. A dead man does not need encouragement. He does not need his self-esteem raised. He needs a resurrection, and a resurrection is precisely the thing he cannot do to himself. The kindest thing this passage does is refuse to lie to you about how sick you were. A doctor who tells a dying man he is fine is not being gentle; he is being cruel, because he is withholding the only diagnosis that leads to a cure. Paul loves this church too much to flatter it.
- **B. This is the great equalizer.** "Even as others." The respectable and the scandalous, the churchgoer and the pagan, the moralist and the addict, stood on exactly the same ground. Before grace there is no elite tier of the almost-good, no partial credit for being less dead than your neighbor. There is only the dead. Which means the ground at the foot of the cross is perfectly level, and no one arrives there with anything to boast about.

### II. The Turn: But God, Rich in Mercy (Ephesians 2:4-9)
Then come two words that carry the weight of the universe. "But God." Paul lets the corpse lie there for three full verses, lets the diagnosis land without relief, and then interrupts the funeral mid-sentence. "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) and hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 2:4-6).

Notice the timing, because the timing is the gospel. He loved us *when we were dead*, not after we improved, not once we cleaned up, not when we showed a flicker of promise he could work with. Paul says it flat in Romans, refusing every version of a God who waits for us to become lovable: "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The rescue landed while we were still enemies, still corpses, still incapable of reaching for it. Jesus put the same truth in the first person, into the mouth of the dead: "he that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life" (John 5:24).

Then Paul closes and bolts every door on self-salvation. "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Even the faith is a gift, the empty hand that receives is itself handed to you. And notice the tense he uses: "by grace are ye saved," in the perfect, a completed act with standing results. Not "are being saved" as if it hung in the balance, not "might be saved" if you keep up your end. It is done, and its results remain. Titus makes the same denial of merit: "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us" (Titus 3:5). Romans slams it shut once and for all: "So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy" (Romans 9:16). Not the willing. Not the running. The mercy.

- **A. Grace is not God helping the willing; it is God raising the dead.** These are two entirely different religions wearing the same vocabulary. One assists your effort and asks you to meet it halfway. The other performs a resurrection you had no part in and could not have contributed to. The first flatters you. The second saves you.
- **B. Boasting is the tell.** Paul says the deliberate design of grace is that no one can boast, the whole thing is arranged to leave you with nothing to brag about. So whenever a Christian's confidence rests even slightly on the quality of his own faith, the depth of his own devotion, the sincerity of his own decision, the boast has crept back in through the side door, and grace has quietly been demoted to assistance.

### III. Living Well When You Contributed Nothing (Ephesians 2:10)
Here is where the passage turns and finds me. I have preached grace with my mouth and lived merit with my body. I have caught myself grading my own week, a good stretch of devotions, a proud private tally of ministry done, a clean run of days, as though the "but God" of my conversion had an expiration date and I was back on works for the maintenance of a standing I first received for free. The dead-then-alive Christian slides back onto the mirror of self-assessment faster than he will ever admit. I have done it from a pulpit, preaching a grace I was busy failing to trust.

The church has had to relearn this in every single generation, because the flesh will not stop resurrecting the ledger. In 1738, an exhausted Anglican priest named John Wesley, a missionary who had crossed an ocean to Georgia trying to save his own soul by discipline and had come home a failure at it, sat reluctantly in a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London while someone read aloud from Luther's preface to Romans. He wrote in his journal that his heart was "strangely warmed," and that he felt he did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation. A religious professional, ordained and devout and rigorous, discovered at that late hour what Ephesians 2 had been saying the whole time, that grace, not effort, raises the dead, and that he had been, until that evening, a corpse in clerical robes.

And then verse 10, which is the answer to the fear that grace makes people lazy. "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). *Poiēma*, his workmanship, his masterpiece, the word from which we get "poem." You are the thing God is making. And the works do not earn the life; the life produces the works, and God prepared them for you in advance, before you were raised, so that even your obedience is grace walking on ahead of you. Paul's own summary of a lifetime of labor was exactly this: "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10). I worked hard. It was not me. Both true, in that order.

- **A. You cannot boast your way in, and you cannot behave your way out.** The same grace that raised you keeps you. Rest there, or you will spend your whole Christian life trying to make payments on a debt God already stamped paid in full at the cross.
- **B. Walk in what he prepared, not to be saved but because you were.** Good works are the evidence of a resurrection that already happened, never the cause of one you are trying to make happen. A dead man's obedience earns him a verdict. A living man's obedience expresses one. And this is the quiet freedom hidden inside the hardest doctrine in the passage: because you did nothing to be raised, there is nothing you can do to be un-raised. The grace that reached a corpse does not run out on the living. The God who loved you when you were dead in your sins does not love you less now that he has made you alive.

Grace from first breath to last.

## The Wall Came Down: One New Man Out of Two (Ephesians 2:11-22)
*How the blood of Christ ended the oldest hostility in the world*

**Text:** Ephesians 2:11-22 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:28 · Colossians 1:20-22 · Isaiah 57:19 · John 10:16 · 1 Peter 2:5 · Acts 10:34-35

Every society runs on a wall. There is always an us and a them, a near and a far, a people who belong by right and a people who are tolerated at the edge. Our post-Christian culture believes it has finally outgrown this, that it is the enlightened, arrived generation that at last sees past tribe. It has not. It has only redrawn the wall and relabeled the sides, sorting people now by politics and class and cause instead of by blood and religion, and calling the new partitions justice. Paul writes to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles in a city famous across the empire for a temple, and he tells them that the deepest division the ancient world knew, a division backed, unlike ours, by God's own revealed law, has been demolished. Not softened. Not managed with better manners. Torn down at the foundation, by blood.

### I. Remember How Far Off You Were (Ephesians 2:11-12)
Paul makes them look back before he lets them celebrate. "Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision... that at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world" (Ephesians 2:11-12).

Five deprivations, stacked one on the next like stones. Without Christ. Alien from the commonwealth. Stranger to the covenants. No hope. Without God, *atheoi*, the word behind our "atheist," here meaning not defiant unbelief but sheer godforsaken distance. This was not preacher's exaggeration. In the Jerusalem temple there stood a literal barrier called the *soreg*, a stone partition roughly chest-high dividing the outer court of the Gentiles from the inner courts where only Jews could go. Archaeologists have recovered its warning inscription, carved in Greek, promising death to any foreigner who passed it, the trespasser would bear the guilt for his own execution. The wall was real, it was stone, and it was carved with a threat.

- **A. You cannot grasp grace until you remember the distance.** A gospel that skips the "far off" produces Christians who feel entitled rather than astonished, people who assume they belong and cannot understand why others do not fall in line. Paul deliberately makes them remember the alienation, the exclusion, the hopelessness, so that the reconciliation, when it comes in the next verse, lands with the weight of a stunned reprieve rather than the shrug of an assumed right.
- **B. "Without God in the world" is the modern condition, not just the ancient one.** The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his 2007 book *A Secular Age*, described the West's slow migration from a world where belief in God was the unquestioned air everyone breathed to a world where belief is only one option among many and God feels absent by default, what he called the immanent frame, a life lived as if the ceiling were closed. Paul names that exact ache centuries early, *atheoi*, without God in the world, and locates it not as a modern achievement but as the universal human starting place that grace finds and reverses.

### II. But Now, Made Near by Blood (Ephesians 2:13-18)
"But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13). There is Paul's "but now", the hinge on which the whole letter swings, the same reversal as the "but God" of the verses just before. And the mechanism is blood, again, always. Nearness was not achieved by dialogue, diplomacy, education, or the passage of enlightened time. It was purchased, at a cross, at cost.

"For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances" (Ephesians 2:14-15). *To mesotoichon tou phragmou*, the middle wall of the fence, the dividing barrier. Paul is looking straight at that temple *soreg* and saying Christ pulled it down, not with a decree from a distance, but in his own body, in his own crucified flesh. And the purpose runs beyond mere ceasefire: "to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace" (Ephesians 2:15). Not a Jew grudgingly tolerating a Gentile across a lowered fence. A third thing entirely, *kainon anthrōpon*, one new humanity, that had never existed on the earth before.

And that phrase, "the law of commandments contained in ordinances," is not Paul waving off the moral law of God. He means the whole ceremonial apparatus that had marked Jew off from Gentile, the food laws, the festival calendar, the circumcision that named the covenant people over against the nations. It had done its God-given work of keeping Israel distinct until the Messiah came. Now the Messiah has come, and the barrier that once separated has done its job and is set aside, its purpose fulfilled rather than merely cancelled. The prophets had promised it. Isaiah, centuries before, heard the Lord say, "Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the LORD; and I will heal him" (Isaiah 57:19), the very far-and-near language Paul now fills with meaning. Jesus said it in the sheepfold: "other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd" (John 10:16). Peter learned it, against every instinct, on a rooftop in Joppa: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him" (Acts 10:34-35). And Paul's own summary is Galatians 3:28, "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

- **A. The cross reconciles vertically and horizontally at once.** "And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby" (Ephesians 2:16). The same act that makes you right with God makes you one with his other children, the vertical and the horizontal are a single beam. You cannot be genuinely reconciled to the Father and remain at war with those he has adopted. The same nails did both jobs, and you do not get to accept one and refuse the other.
- **B. Access, not just amnesty.** "For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father" (Ephesians 2:18). This is more than a pardon that lets you off. The barred court is opened; the threatening inscription is voided; the Gentile who once faced death for crossing the line now walks all the way in, by the Spirit, to the Father himself. And note the mechanism of the access, "by one Spirit." The same Spirit indwells the former Jew and the former Gentile, which is why the wall cannot be rebuilt in good conscience. To hold a man at arm's length whom the Spirit has brought near is to contradict the Spirit who now lives in you both.

### III. Living Well as One Body in a Culture of Walls
Here is my confession, and it is not a comfortable one. I have preached reconciliation from the front and protected my own quiet walls in the back. I have called my preferences discernment and my tribalism conviction, and I have sorted people into near and far by things Christ never authorized, politics, class, style, education, the hundred small partitions a comfortable church builds and then baptizes as wisdom. I have stood inside a body Christ died to make one and helped keep the *soreg* standing in the parking lot, in the small talk, in who gets welcomed and who gets tolerated. We tear down the temple wall on Sunday morning and rebuild it by Tuesday over lesser things, and we call the rebuilding prudence.

The church has failed here in ways that should still make us grieve rather than lecture. In the American South, for more than a century, professing Christians read Ephesians 2 aloud on Sunday and then walked out to churches, schools, and lunch counters divided by a color line they defended from the same open Bible. In April of 1963, writing from a jail cell in Birmingham, a pastor named Martin Luther King observed that eleven o'clock on Sunday morning was the most segregated hour in America. A wall Christ abolished in his flesh, patiently rebuilt in his name, by people singing his hymns. That is not merely a Southern sin or a dead sin from a closed chapter. It is the human sin, the wall-building reflex, and it is mine.

And the answer this passage gives is not a better program or a more current vocabulary. The answer is the blood in verse 13. Paul tells the Colossians that Christ made "peace through the blood of his cross" and reconciled those who "were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works" (Colossians 1:20-21). The wall does not come down because we resolve to be nicer or attend the right seminar. It comes down because a body was broken to make two hostile peoples into one temple, "an holy temple in the Lord... an habitation of God through the Spirit" (Ephesians 2:21-22), living stones, as Peter says, "built up a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:5). We are not renovating an old building. We are the building, and Christ is the cornerstone.

- **A. Name the walls you have baptized.** The partitions you defend most confidently as conviction are precisely the ones most likely to be flesh wearing conviction's clothes. Test them at the cross.
- **B. You are not a guest in this house; you are the house.** Belonging is not something you earn at the door by fitting in. It was purchased at the cross and built into your foundations by the Spirit. And the reconciliation runs deeper than a truce between people who have agreed to get along. Paul says Christ made "one new man," a third humanity that did not exist before, which means the person across the aisle you find hardest to love is not a problem to be tolerated but a fellow stone in the same temple, cut from the same quarry by the same hands. To keep a wall standing between you is to deface something God is building for himself to live in.

Two peoples, one body, no wall.

## The Mystery and the Power: The Church as God's Wisdom on Display (Ephesians 3:1-21)
*What the ordinary local church reveals to the powers of heaven*

**Text:** Ephesians 3:1-21 · **Supporting:** Colossians 1:26-27 · 1 Peter 1:12 · Romans 16:25-26 · 1 Corinthians 2:7 · John 17:23 · 1 Timothy 3:16

The word *mystery* in our culture means a puzzle waiting to be solved, a locked room, a hidden clue, a case you have not cracked yet, a thing that will yield to a clever enough detective. That is not what Paul means, not once, anywhere in the New Testament. In Scripture a mystery is not a riddle you solve by being smart; it is a secret God kept hidden until he himself decided to say it out loud. The initiative is entirely his. And in the third chapter of Ephesians, Paul tells this small, unremarkable congregation something that should have knocked them off their benches, that they are the announcement. Not the audience receiving the mystery. The content of it. In an age that measures a church by its size and its production and its cultural relevance, Paul says the powers of heaven are leaning over the balcony to watch your ordinary congregation, to learn something about God they cannot learn anywhere else in creation.

### I. The Mystery Made Known (Ephesians 3:1-7)
Paul writes as "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" (Ephesians 3:1), a man in chains, and he refuses to call them Rome's chains. He calls them Christ's. Then he describes what has been entrusted to him: "how that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery... which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit" (Ephesians 3:3-5). Hidden in other ages. Revealed now. That is the shape of every biblical mystery, long silence, then disclosure.

And the content of the great mystery is almost anticlimactic to modern ears, until you feel its actual weight: "that the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel" (Ephesians 3:6). That is the secret of the ages. Not a doctrine of the end times, not a hidden Bible code, the outsiders would be brought all the way in. Not as second-class attendees permitted to observe from the back, but as *fellow* heirs, of the *same* body, joint partakers of the promise. Paul calls it in Colossians "the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest to his saints... which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:26-27).

- **A. The gospel was always headed here.** Romans 16:25-26 speaks of "the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, but now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets... made known to all nations for the obedience of faith." God did not improvise the inclusion of the nations when the Jewish mission stalled. He planned it before the world began and held it in deliberate silence until the cross made it possible and the resurrection made it public.
- **B. Even angels leaned in to see it.** Peter says the prophets themselves searched their own writings trying to understand, and that these are "things the angels desire to look into" (1 Peter 1:12). The verb Peter uses pictures someone stooping down and craning to peer into something just out of reach. The reunion of a fractured humanity into one body under one Lord is a spectacle the unfallen heavenly host studies with longing, bending over the edge of heaven to watch it happen in the mess of an ordinary congregation. What we yawn through on a Sunday, they lean in to see. And the same disclosure runs through Paul's own writing, "which none of the princes of this world knew", the great secret was hidden even from the powers until the church revealed it.

### II. The Church, God's Wisdom on Display (Ephesians 3:8-13)
Now Paul says plainly why the mystery was revealed through the church, and it is the most staggering claim in the letter. "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8). And then the purpose clause that should reorganize how you think about your congregation: "to the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God" (Ephesians 3:10).

*Polupoikilos sophia*, the many-colored, many-textured, intricately variegated wisdom of God. The word was used of an embroidered cloth woven with many threads or a garden of many-hued flowers. It is the picture of a single design so intricate that no one thread accounts for its beauty; the wisdom is in the weaving. And the audience for this display is not the seeker down the street or the demographic Paul is trying to reach. The audience is the principalities and powers, the unseen authorities, the watching spiritual order, angelic and otherwise. God is mounting an exhibition of his wisdom before the cosmos itself, and the exhibit, the object on display in the gallery, is the church. Specifically, it is Jews and Gentiles, ancient enemies with every earthly reason to despise each other, sitting together in one body, sharing one table, loving one another with a love no political theory or social program could ever produce. Paul told the Corinthians he preached "the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory" (1 Corinthians 2:7).

- **A. Your local church is an argument aimed at heaven.** The reconciled congregation, mismatched, undramatic, quietly faithful, forgiving each other again on a Tuesday, is God's own evidence, presented to the powers, that his wisdom outstrips theirs and his gospel does what their kingdoms never could. This is precisely why unity is not a matter of program preference or personality management. It is the sermon the church is preaching to the angels every week, whether it means to or not.
- **B. Access is the point, not spectacle.** "In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him" (Ephesians 3:12). The display of wisdom is not a performance staged for its own sake. The reconciled people are a reconciled people precisely because they now walk freely, boldly, into the very presence of the God they were once far from. This is the ache buried under a whole secular age, the sense that whatever door once stood open to the transcendent is now closed and painted over. Paul says the door is not closed. It was opened by blood, and the people who were furthest off now walk through it with confidence, which is itself the wisdom of God on display before the powers who assumed no such door existed.

### III. Living Well Under a Love Beyond Knowing (Ephesians 3:14-21)
So Paul bows. Having climbed to the throne room and the watching powers, he goes to his knees. "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 3:14). And he prays "that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; that Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith" (Ephesians 3:16-17). Then the reach that finally breaks the sentence wide open: "that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; and to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God" (Ephesians 3:18-19).

To know the love that surpasses knowing. Paul is not confused, and it is not a contradiction. He means the love of Christ is so vast in every dimension that grasping it is a lifetime's work that still never reaches the edge, you spend eternity moving further in and never arrive at the wall, because there is no wall. This is the answer to the deepest modern hunger. A culture that keeps trying to know itself into wholeness, to therapize and analyze and understand its way to peace, is told by Paul that the peace it wants was never going to come from self-knowledge. It comes from being known, and rooted, and held by a love with no measurable boundary.

Here is the confession. I have led churches that treated unity as a nicety and attendance as the scoreboard, and I have grieved the reconciled body of Christ over things that would embarrass an angel, style, turf, wounded pride dressed as principle. The church at Ephesus was small and poor and watched by heaven. In our own anxious hunger for relevance and size, we have too often reached for everything except the one thing the powers are actually watching for, a people whose love for one another cannot be accounted for by any means but Christ.

The early church knew exactly what it possessed, even under threat. In the late second century, the North African writer Tertullian recorded the astonished words pagans used of Christians who had no earthly reason on earth to belong to one another, different classes, different nations, former enemies now sharing bread: "See how they love one another." That was the display. That was the manifold wisdom of God made visible to a hostile empire, not superior argument, not spectacle, not power, but a reconciled love the watching world could not explain. It is the answer to Jesus' own prayer the night before he died, that his people would be "made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me" (John 17:23). The church united is the proof of the Father's love, offered to a doubting world.

- **A. Guard the unity, because it is the sermon.** What you privately dismiss as internal church politics, heaven reads as public testimony about the character of God.
- **B. Ask to be filled, not merely informed.** Paul prays for the fullness of God to dwell in them, not for more facts about him. The whole prayer ends not in application but in worship: "unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end" (Ephesians 3:21). Note where the glory lands, in the church. Not around it, not despite it, but in it. The ordinary congregation you might be tempted to leave over an offense is the very place God has chosen to be glorified before heaven and earth. Before you dismiss the local church as small and disappointing, remember who is watching it, and why.

The church is God's wisdom on display.

## Walk Worthy, Grow Up: Unity Kept and the Body Built (Ephesians 4:1-16)
*The unity you are commanded to keep is the unity Christ already made*

**Text:** Ephesians 4:1-16 · **Supporting:** John 17:21 · 1 Corinthians 12:12-13 · Philippians 2:1-3 · Colossians 2:19 · Psalm 68:18 · 1 Corinthians 12:7

There is a lie that lives comfortably in a post-Christian culture, and it has crept into the church wearing church clothes and carrying a lanyard. The lie is that unity is something we build. We hold the summits, draft the statements, launch the initiatives, run the campaigns, and produce, with enough effort and the right techniques and a good enough facilitator, a togetherness we manufactured ourselves and can take credit for. Paul begins the entire practical half of Ephesians by pulling that assumption up by the root. He does not tell the church to build its unity. He tells it to keep a unity that already exists, already given, already fact. And the distance between building and keeping is the distance between exhaustion and rest, between a project you own and a gift you steward.

### I. Keep the Unity You Did Not Make (Ephesians 4:1-6)
"I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called" (Ephesians 4:1). The whole back half of this letter turns on that one verb, *walk*, *peripateō*, the ordinary daily conduct of a life, step after step, in the actual traffic of Monday. Paul has spent three chapters on what is true; now he moves to how you walk. And the first mark of a worthy walk is not doctrinal precision or ministry output or spiritual achievement. It is character: "with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love" (Ephesians 4:2). Humility. Gentleness. Patience. Bearing with people who are hard to bear.

Then the command itself: "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3). *Tērein*, to guard, to keep watch over, to preserve intact something already in your possession. You cannot preserve what you were never given. Paul grounds the whole thing in verses 4 through 6 with a sevenfold hammer that leaves no room for argument: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." Seven ones. The unity of the church is first a fact about the nature of the one God before it is ever a task for the church. You are one because he is one.

- **A. Character comes before competence, always.** Paul spends an entire verse on lowliness and patience and forbearance before he says a single word about gifts or growth or ministry structure. This is not incidental ordering. He told the Philippians the same thing, and grounded it in the same place: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Philippians 2:3). A gifted church without lowliness will tear its own unity to pieces, and no amount of talent, no excellence of preaching or music or program, ever covers for a proud spirit. The making of the body always begins with the unmaking of the ego. It is worth noticing that *tapeinophrosunē*, the word for lowliness Paul uses, was not a virtue in the ancient world at all, the Greeks despised it as the posture of a slave. The gospel took the world's contempt and made it the first mark of a Christian.
- **B. This is the unity Christ prayed for the night before he died.** In the upper room, hours from the cross, Jesus prayed "that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me" (John 17:21). Paul is telling the church to guard, with all diligence, the very thing the Son knelt and asked the Father to give. To fracture it carelessly is to spend what Christ purchased with prayer and blood.

### II. The Ascended Christ Gives Gifts to Grow the Body (Ephesians 4:7-16)
Unity is not uniformity, so Paul immediately turns to diversity, lest anyone hear "one" and think "identical." "But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ" (Ephesians 4:7). One body, many gifts. He then quotes Psalm 68, "When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men" (Ephesians 4:8, from Psalm 68:18). The image is a conquering king ascending in triumph to his throne, and instead of merely collecting spoils, distributing them. And the spoils the ascended Christ gives to his church are not things. They are people: "he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers" (Ephesians 4:11). The gifted leaders are themselves Christ's gift to the body.

But notice, and do not miss, the purpose of these gifted leaders, it is emphatically not to do the ministry while everyone else watches from the seats. "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ" (Ephesians 4:12). *Katartismos*, the equipping, the outfitting, the same word used for setting a broken bone and for mending a torn fishing net. The leader's God-given job is to get the whole body working, every joint supplying, so that the church can grow up, "that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness" (Ephesians 4:14), but "may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ" (Ephesians 4:15). Paul names two marks of the child here, the child is unstable, blown about by every new teaching, and the child is gullible, prey to the con man. A church of perpetual spectators stays a church of perpetual children, easily deceived precisely because it was never equipped to stand.

- **A. Gifts are given for the body, not for the self.** Paul told the Corinthians the same: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal" (1 Corinthians 12:7), and "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body... and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:13). Your gift is not your platform to build, your identity to protect, or your ministry to own. It is your assignment to the whole, given to you, but for them.
- **B. Growth flows down from the head, organically, not from the machinery.** "From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth... maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love" (Ephesians 4:16). Paul warns the Colossians about the man "not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered... increaseth with the increase of God" (Colossians 2:19). A church grows the way a living body grows, from its connection to the head, nourished through its joints, never by programming bolted on from outside.

### III. Living Well as a Body That Refuses to Stay a Child
I have to confess the exact shape of my own failure here, because it is a pastor's failure. I have treated unity as something I could engineer with the right structure, and I have treated ministry as something the professionals perform while the congregation sits and consumes and evaluates. I have kept people children, dependent, spectating, unequipped, arriving to receive and leaving unchanged, because, if I am honest, a passive audience is easier to manage than an equipped and mobilized body. The pastor who does all the ministry himself has not served the church. He has stunted it. He has starved the joints so the head could keep the credit. I have done exactly that.

The church learned this lesson the hard way once, at enormous cost, and had to fight to recover it. By the early sixteenth century the whole Western church had settled into a rigid two-tier arrangement: the clergy did the holy work, read the Scripture, administered grace, mediated God, while the laity watched from a distance in a language they could not understand. The Reformers recovered what they called the priesthood of all believers, which is nothing more or less than what Ephesians 4 says outright, that Christ gave leaders to equip the saints for the work, not to replace them in it, and that the body only ever grows when every joint supplies its part. It was not a new idea invented in Wittenberg or Geneva. It was a return, five hundred years overdue, to this very paragraph.

And underneath all of it stands the head, which is the point Paul will not let go. The unity we are told to keep is his gift. The gifts we exercise are his distribution from his ascension throne. The growth we long for is growth "into him." Paul refuses at every turn to let the church become a self-improvement club with a spiritual coat of paint, a religious project we manage for our own ends. Everything runs to Christ and comes from Christ. Even the beloved phrase "speaking the truth in love," so often quoted alone as a rule for hard conversations, is fixed inside a sentence about the whole body growing up into its head (Ephesians 4:15). The truth we speak is meant to grow people toward him, not merely to win an argument.

- **A. Get equipped, then get to work.** If you have spent years as an audience, waiting to be fed and evaluating the meal, you have quietly missed the actual ministry Christ gave the church in order to grow you into. The pew was never meant to be a permanent address.
- **B. Guard the unity as a stewardship, not a mood.** You did not make it, and you have no authority to break it over your preferences. Christ prayed it into being and purchased it with blood. Handle it like something that costs. The lowliness and meekness and longsuffering of verse 2 are not soft add-ons to the real work of the church; they are the real work, the daily labor of keeping intact what Christ has given. A church does not usually die of heresy. It dies of a thousand small refusals to forbear one another in love, and every one of those refusals is a hand laid on something Christ prayed for the night before he died.

Unity is kept, not built.

## Off With the Old, On With the New: Learning to Wear a New Self (Ephesians 4:17-5:21)
*The new life is not self-improvement, it is putting on a self God already created*

**Text:** Ephesians 4:17-5:21 · **Supporting:** Colossians 3:9-10 · Romans 6:6 · Galatians 5:22-23 · 2 Corinthians 5:17 · Romans 12:2 · 1 Thessalonians 5:18

Our culture believes in reinvention with a religious intensity. You rebrand, you upgrade, you optimize, you become the best version of yourself through effort and willpower and the right morning routine and the right app. It is the oldest promise in the world dressed in the newest clothes. And it fails, reliably, because you cannot repair a self from inside the very self that needs repairing, the tool and the broken thing are the same object. Paul spends the long central section of Ephesians on the practical Christian life, on what changed people actually do, and he does something the entire reinvention industry can never do. He does not tell you to improve the old self. He tells you it is dead, already crucified, and that there is a new self to put on, one you did not manufacture, one God created after his own likeness. The Christian life is not becoming a better version of the old you. It is learning to wear what you have already become.

### I. Put Off the Old Self and Its Corruption (Ephesians 4:17-24)
Paul draws the line between the two lives hard and dark: "That ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart" (Ephesians 4:17-18). This is the old life mapped in full, futile thinking, darkened understanding, a heart gone hard past feeling, "who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness" (Ephesians 4:19). And then the great and total contrast, four words that turn the passage: "But ye have not so learned Christ" (Ephesians 4:20). Note what the Christian learned. Not a technique. Not a moral code. A person. You learned Christ.

The command comes wrapped in the image of clothing, because that is exactly how transformation works day to day. "That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Ephesians 4:22-24). *Apothesthai* and *endusasthai*, take off and put on, the way you peel off a garment caked in the day's filth and dress in something clean. Colossians runs the identical image: "ye have put off the old man with his deeds; and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Colossians 3:9-10).

- **A. The old self is not renovated; it is crucified.** Paul is blunt about this in Romans: "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin" (Romans 6:6). You do not rehabilitate the old man, send him to counseling, teach him better habits. You bury him, because he is already dead in Christ. Paul's whole summary of it is 2 Corinthians 5:17, "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
- **B. The new self is created, not achieved.** Look closely at verse 24: the new man is "created", a divine act, in the passive voice, done to you, not by you. This is the fault line running between the gospel and every reinvention scheme ever sold. Reinvention says: build yourself into someone better by your own effort. The gospel says: God created a new self in you, now learn to wear it. One exhausts you with a project you can never finish. The other hands you an identity you could never have earned.

### II. Walk in Love, Walk in Light, Be Filled (Ephesians 4:25-5:21)
Paul refuses to let holiness float in the abstract, so he gets immediately and almost embarrassingly specific, because a new self shows up in the oldest, most ordinary places, the mouth, the temper, the wallet, the marriage bed, the hours after dark. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another" (Ephesians 4:25). "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Ephesians 4:28), notice the aim of the reformed thief is not merely to stop stealing but to have surplus to give away. "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying" (Ephesians 4:29). "And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30), the Spirit is a person who can be grieved, not a force to be operated or a battery to be tapped.

Then Paul gathers it all under two governing images. Walk in love: "And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God" (Ephesians 5:2). Walk in light: "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light" (Ephesians 5:8). Not, walk toward the light, you are light now, so walk like it. And then the engine that makes the whole new life run: "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). The fruit of that filling is exactly what Paul lists to the Galatians, "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance" (Galatians 5:22-23), a harvest grown by the Spirit, not a product manufactured by clenched willpower.

- **A. The new self is worn in the small and the daily, or it is not worn at all.** Not lying. Working in order to give. Guarding the tongue. Refusing to grieve the Spirit. Being filled instead of numbed. Paul will not permit sanctification to stay a lofty idea; he drags it down to your hands and your mouth and your Thursday. Holiness you cannot locate in your ordinary conduct is holiness you do not actually have.
- **B. Filling replaces the old anesthetics.** The contrast in verse 18 is deliberate and it exposes us. A post-Christian world runs on numbing, the drink, the endless scroll, the substance, the noise, the distraction that keeps us from feeling the weight of our own lives. Paul sets the counterfeit filling against the real one: do not deaden yourself with wine, be filled with the Spirit. "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). The Spirit-filled life is not a subdued, joyless, careful life. It is an awakened one, alive to God rather than anesthetized against everything.

### III. Living Well When the Old Self Keeps Reaching for Its Clothes
Here is the confession, and it is not a comfortable one to make from a pulpit. I have preached "put off the old man" on a Sunday and reached back into the closet for the old garments before the sermon was even cold, the sharp word to someone I love, the private resentment I nurse and justify, the numbing habit I dress up and call rest. The old self is dead, genuinely crucified, but it has muscle memory, and I have worn its rags long after Christ told me plainly they were rags. Sanctification, I have had to learn slowly, is not the heroic project of becoming someone new by force of will. It is the daily, humbling work of learning to stop reflexively dressing like the corpse I already left in the grave.

The Christian tradition named this dynamic with brutal precision long before the therapists did. Augustine, writing his *Confessions* around the year 397, described his own bondage to sin not as an occasional lapse a little more effort could fix, but as a set of ingrained habits with a real gravitational pull, "the chain of habit," he called it, a bondage he could not break simply by wanting to break it, only by the intervening grace of God. That is the honest, unflattering texture of the new life, and it is a mercy that Scripture tells the truth about it. The new self is real and created and fully yours in Christ. And the old self still reaches for its clothes every single morning. The daily war is not to earn a new man you do not have; it is to stop, again and again, putting on the old one you do not need.

And the power to win that daily war is not, finally, willpower, which is exactly the resource reinvention runs on and exactly the resource that runs out. Romans 12:2 says be "transformed by the renewing of your mind", the mind renewed, the self recreated, both passive verbs, both the work of God worked on you. The connection to Christ throughout this passage is not decoration you could remove. The new man is "created" after Christ; the walk in love is patterned on the fact that Christ "gave himself for us"; you are light only "in the Lord." You do not walk as a child of light by gritting your teeth and trying harder. You walk that way because, in the Lord, you have actually become one.

- **A. Stop asking how to improve the old self. Bury it.** Every ounce of energy you pour into renovating the corpse is energy stolen from the far simpler work of wearing the new man Christ already made.
- **B. Be filled, or you will be numbed.** There is no neutral third option, no coasting middle. The self that is not being filled with the Spirit will inevitably reach for something else to deaden it. Choose your filling, because you will have one. And notice the mercy hidden in the imperative: "be filled" is passive. It is not a command to work yourself up into holiness by effort but an invitation to be filled by Another. The new self you are learning to wear was created by God, and the power to wear it is supplied by God, and the only thing left to you is to stop reaching for the rags in the closet and let yourself be clothed.

You are not who you were.

## Christ and the Church at Home: The Gospel Reaches the Kitchen Table (Ephesians 5:22-6:9)
*Every household relationship is reshaped by one mystery, Christ and his bride*

**Text:** Ephesians 5:22-6:9 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:24 · Colossians 3:18-4:1 · Philippians 2:5-8 · 1 Peter 3:7 · Mark 10:45 · Galatians 3:28

There is a test for whether a theology is real or merely admired. Bring it home. Put it at the kitchen table, into the marriage, into the way a father speaks to a tired child at the end of a long day, into the way authority actually gets used behind a closed front door where no congregation is watching and no reputation is at stake. Most religion never survives that test. It stays in the sanctuary, warm and abstract and applauded, and quietly dies on the drive home. Paul refuses, flatly, to let the gospel stay in the pew. He takes the single highest mystery in the entire letter, Christ and his church, the union the whole cosmos was built to display, and drives it straight into the household, into the exact relationships where most of us do our worst real damage and where most of us most desperately need grace.

### I. The Whole Household Ordered Under Christ (Ephesians 5:22-6:9)
Paul introduces the entire household section with one governing command that lands on absolutely everyone before it is ever applied to anyone in particular: "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" (Ephesians 5:21). Mutual submission under Christ is the whole atmosphere of the Christian home; what follows are the specific shapes it takes in specific stations. Wives to their own husbands (5:22). Husbands giving themselves entirely for their wives (5:25). Children obeying parents in the Lord (6:1). Fathers not provoking their children (6:4). Servants and masters, both answering to the very same Lord above (6:5-9). Every station is addressed. No one is left merely to command.

And the center of gravity in the whole passage is not the wife's submission, where the culture wars have parked their tanks; it is the husband's cross. "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Ephesians 5:25). The measure Paul hands the husband is a crucifixion. He is not describing a man who presides and rules and is served; he is describing a man who dies for the good of another. Colossians compresses the entire household code into a few lines: "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them. Children, obey your parents in all things... Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged" (Colossians 3:18-21).

- **A. Headship is defined by self-giving, not self-assertion.** The pattern the husband is handed is Philippians 2, Christ, "who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant... and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:6-8). A man who reads Ephesians 5 as a license to command and be obeyed has read straight past the only verb in the sentence that actually defines his role: *gave himself*. His authority is the authority of a man laying his life down. Paul even sets the aim of that love, Christ gave himself "that he might sanctify and cleanse" his bride, "that he might present it to himself a glorious church" (Ephesians 5:26-27). The husband's love is not merely affection; it is a love that aims at the flourishing and holiness of the one he loves, at her good and not his comfort.
- **B. Authority in the home always answers upward.** "And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him" (Ephesians 6:9). Every single station of authority Paul names has a Master standing over it. No father, no husband, no employer stands at the top of anything. Christ does. And that one fact reframes every use of power under every Christian roof, you will answer for how you used it.

### II. The Mystery Underneath the Marriage (Ephesians 5:31-33)
Paul reaches all the way back to the garden and quotes the first marriage: "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh" (Ephesians 5:31, quoting Genesis 2:24). And then he says the thing that reveals what marriage was for from the very beginning: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32).

Marriage, Paul says, was never merely a social contract, a means of companionship, or an arrangement for raising children, though it is all of those. From the first pages of Scripture it was a living picture, a walking parable, a husband and wife becoming one flesh precisely because they were made to shadow a greater union: Christ becoming one with his people. The word here, *mustērion*, is the same word from chapter 3, a secret God kept hidden and then unveiled. And the secret unveiled here is that human marriage was always, from Eden forward, pointing past itself to a union larger than itself. This reorders the whole modern conversation about marriage, which assumes marriage exists to make the two people happy and dissolves the moment it stops doing so. Paul says marriage was built to display something, the covenant faithfulness of Christ to a people who did not deserve it, and a display does not get abandoned the first hard winter. It is precisely in the staying, the not-leaving, the loving of a spouse who is difficult to love, that the picture of Christ and his church is preached. Peter grounds the husband's tenderness in exactly this reality, charging husbands to dwell with their wives "according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered" (1 Peter 3:7).

- **A. Your marriage is a sermon whether you ever meant it to be one or not.** If Christ loved his bride by giving himself up for her, then a husband's harshness or a wife's contempt is not merely a domestic problem, it preaches a false gospel from the pulpit of the home, tells a watching world and watching children a lie about how Christ treats his people. The stakes of the kitchen table are not merely relational. They are theological.
- **B. The equal dignity of everyone in the household stands underneath the differing roles.** "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). Paul orders the household with real distinctions of calling, and he never once flattens the worth of a single person in it. Different roles, one grace, no respect of persons. The wife submits to no one's contempt; the servant is no one's inferior in Christ.

### III. Living Well at the Table Where No One Is Watching
Here is the confession, and it is the hardest one in this whole letter for me to make out loud. I have preached Christ's self-giving, self-emptying love from a pulpit with real feeling and then come home and used my authority to take rather than to give. I have been patient and gentle with a congregation of near-strangers and short and impatient with my own sons. I have told husbands, in sermons, to love as Christ loved the church, and then let bitterness quietly curdle behind my own front door where no elder and no member could ever see it. The gospel that cannot survive my kitchen table is not a gospel I have actually believed all the way down. It is a performance I put on for the sanctuary and take off in the driveway.

And the command in verse 4 cuts a man like me clean open: "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). I was raised without a father. I have spent my whole adult life quietly afraid of provoking my sons the way an absence once provoked me, of passing down a wound rather than a blessing. Paul knew exactly what unchecked authority does to a child. In the Roman world into which he wrote, the *patria potestas*, the father's power, granted a man near-absolute legal authority over his household; he could, in law, sell a child into slavery, and in the oldest reaches of that law, even take a child's life. Into that brutal, authoritarian arrangement Paul writes a single stunning line of restraint: fathers, do not provoke. The gospel walked into the most autocratic institution of the ancient world and told the man holding all the power to lay it down for the good of the weakest people under his roof.

That is the whole pattern, and it flows from one source and one source only. "Even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." The Lord who had every right to command chose instead to kneel and to serve and to die, "for even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).
