The Christian home is meant to run on that identical current. Not power hoarded and defended. Power spent, poured out, given away, for the ones who live under your roof and cannot repay you.

- **A. Preach the gospel where no one applauds.** The truest measure of your theology is not the version of you that stands in the pew or the pulpit. It is the version that shows up, tired and unwatched, at the dinner table.
- **B. Use every ounce of authority you have to give, never to take.** That is the only headship, the only fatherhood, the only mastery the New Testament recognizes as Christian. Any other kind is simply the world's power with a Bible verse taped to it. And the reason to spend your authority rather than hoard it is not that authority is bad, Paul does not abolish it, but that your home is a picture of Christ and his church, and Christ never once used his authority to take. He used it, every time, to give himself away. A father who grasps that will find that the hardest command in the passage, "provoke not your children," stops being a restriction and becomes the shape of a love he is finally free to give.

The gospel reaches the kitchen table.

## Standing in the Strength of the Lord: The Armor and the Real Enemy (Ephesians 6:10-24)
*Why the Christian's whole task is to stand, in a strength that is not his own*

**Text:** Ephesians 6:10-24 · **Supporting:** 2 Corinthians 10:3-5 · Isaiah 59:17 · Romans 13:12 · 2 Chronicles 20:15 · James 4:7 · Zechariah 4:6

A post-Christian culture holds a remarkably thin account of evil. It believes in bad systems, bad chemistry, and bad upbringings, and it believes, at bottom, that with enough policy and therapy and education and effort we can eventually engineer the trouble away, because the trouble is finally a solvable problem in a closed material world. Paul closes the most theological letter he ever wrote by telling a small congregation something that account cannot hold: that the real war is one they cannot see, waged against an enemy their categories do not even include, and that their entire assignment in that war comes down to a single unglamorous verb. Not conquer. Not advance. Not win. Stand. And even the standing is not done in their own strength. What reads at first like a rousing battle cry turns out, on closer reading, to be a summons to depend.

### I. The Battle Is Not Against Flesh and Blood (Ephesians 6:10-12)
"Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might" (Ephesians 6:10). The very first word Paul says about spiritual warfare is a word about strength, and it is pointedly not the believer's own strength. *Endunamousthe en Kuriō*, be strengthened in the Lord, a passive imperative, a command to receive rather than to generate. Then the assignment: "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Ephesians 6:11). Against the *methodeia*, the schemes, the strategies, the cunning of an intelligent enemy.

And then Paul names the actual front line, and it is not where we instinctively look. "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places" (Ephesians 6:12). The people who frustrate and wound and oppose you are not the enemy. The difficult spouse, the hostile coworker, the political opponent you have learned to loathe, flesh and blood, every one of them, and not one of them the real war. Paul told the Corinthians the identical thing: "For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: (for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds)" (2 Corinthians 10:3-4).

- **A. Naming the wrong enemy loses the war before it is even fought.** Spend all your rage and strategy on the human being standing in front of you, and the actual powers working behind the curtain go entirely untouched and undisturbed. The very moment you make another person your ultimate enemy, you have already been outmaneuvered, you are fighting a decoy while the real assault continues unopposed. This is why a bitter, combative Christian, however right his cause, is a defeated one.
- **B. The strength is borrowed, and that borrowing is the entire point.** Israel heard it from Jahaziel when a vast army bore down on them: "Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's" (2 Chronicles 20:15). Zechariah heard it as the word of the Lord over a work too big for him: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). The war is not won on the strength of your resolve. It is won on your knees, in a strength on loan.

### II. The Whole Armor of God (Ephesians 6:13-17)
Paul lists the equipment piece by piece, and the crucial thing to see is that every single piece is God's own. "Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness" (Ephesians 6:14). "And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace" (Ephesians 6:15). "Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (Ephesians 6:16). "And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Ephesians 6:17).

This armor is not Paul's clever invention, drawn merely from watching the Roman soldier chained to his wrist in the prison. It is God's own armor, worn first by God himself. Isaiah, seven centuries earlier, saw the Lord dress for battle to save a people who could not save themselves: "For he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke" (Isaiah 59:17). The Warrior in Isaiah armors up because "there was no man" to intervene, no one else could win the battle, so God himself put on the armor and fought it. When Paul tells the church to put on the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, he is telling them to wear the very armor God wears, to be clothed in his righteousness, guarded by his salvation. And notice that every piece is either defensive or rooted in truth, except one. There is a single offensive weapon in the whole arsenal: the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, the very weapon the Lord Jesus himself wielded against the tempter in the wilderness, meeting each assault not with argument or willpower but with "it is written."

- **A. The armor is not a technique to master; it is Christ to put on.** Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, salvation, faith, these are not spiritual accessories the believer generates by discipline. They are the things Christ is and the things Christ gives. Paul makes the connection explicit to the Romans: "let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light... But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 13:12, 14). To armor up for this war is, finally, to put on Christ himself.
- **B. The one offensive weapon is the word.** In a culture that trusts its own reasoning above all else and treats Scripture as one voice among many, Paul hands the church a single Scripture-shaped sword and says: this, and only this, is your weapon of attack. We do not out-clever the principalities. We do not defeat the powers with sharper arguments of our own making. We answer them precisely the way our Lord did in the desert, "it is written."

### III. Living Well as People Who Stand and Pray (Ephesians 6:18-24)
And then, after all the martial imagery of armor and swords and battle lines, Paul's actual final instruction is not a charge to attack but a posture to hold: "Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints" (Ephesians 6:18). The fully armed soldier's chief and constant action turns out to be prayer. James says the sequence plainly and refuses to let us reverse it: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you" (James 4:7). Submission to God comes first. Then, and only then, resistance to the enemy. Reverse the order, resist in your own strength before you have submitted, and you will simply lose.

Here is the confession. I have fought the wrong enemy for most of my life. I have treated people as the obstacle, the difficult member, the opposing voice, the flesh-and-blood face of my own frustration, and I have poured out on them the fight that belonged entirely against the powers standing behind them. And I have tried, again and again, to stand in my own strength, armored in nothing but my competence and my will and my certainty, and I have gone down every time, because the strength was never mine to spend in the first place. I have preached the whole armor of God from a pulpit and then walked straight out into the battle wearing nothing but my own confidence, and wondered why I fell.

The church carries a long memory of what this standing actually costs. On April 18, 1521, a monk named Martin Luther stood before the assembled power of the Holy Roman Empire at the Diet of Worms, ordered by emperor and church to recant everything he had written, and said he could not and would not go against a conscience captive to the word of God, "Here I stand; I can do no other." He had no army behind him, no earthly power, no political weight to throw, no weapon in his hand but the Scripture in his heart. The sword of the Spirit against the assembled principalities of an empire. That is the exact picture Ephesians 6 paints: a believer with no earthly advantage whatsoever, standing in a borrowed strength, holding one weapon, refusing to fall.

And that borrowed strength has a name and, underneath the name, a cross. The devil is a defeated enemy, and the reason he is defeated is that the head has already crushed him, the resurrection Paul celebrated back in chapter 1, where Christ was raised and seated over all principality and power, is the victory that chapter 6 simply stands inside. We do not fight our way toward a victory still in doubt. We stand our ground inside a victory already won at Golgotha and sealed at the empty tomb. Paul ends the whole letter exactly where he began it, in unearned grace: "Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity. Amen" (Ephesians 6:24).

- **A. Stop fighting the people. Fight on your knees.** The person standing in front of you is not your enemy, and you will go on losing this war, however righteous you feel, until you actually believe that and pray accordingly.
- **B. Stand in his strength, not yours.** The armor is God's. The sword is God's word. The battle is God's. And the only thing genuinely left for you to do is hold the ground that the cross has already won. Which reframes the whole command. "Stand" is not a heroic call to hold the line by sheer grit until you are overrun. It is a command to remain, planted, inside a victory that was secured without you and cannot be lost by you, to refuse to abandon ground that Christ already took. The enemy's entire strategy is to convince you the outcome is still in doubt so that you will fight in your own strength and fall. It is not in doubt. Stand.

Stand. The strength is his.
